BOUNDARY LINE AGREEMENT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105

DECLARATION OF ADJOINING OWNERS AND THE AGREED BOUNDARY LINE
Jordan Alex Lee ("Party One"), owner of the real property located at 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105, described as Lot 5, Block 12, per map recorded in Book 40, Page 15, San Francisco County Records ("Parcel One"), and Taylor Morgan ("Party Two"), owner of the real property located at 502 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105, described as Lot 6, Block 12, per map recorded in Book 40, Page 15, San Francisco County Records ("Parcel Two"), are owners of adjoining parcels of real property in San Francisco County County, California. Parcel One is also identified by Assessor's Parcel Number 123-456-789, and Parcel Two is also identified by Assessor's Parcel Number 123-456-790, each provided for identification only and not as part of either parcel's legal description.

Party One and Party Two state that uncertainty exists, or has existed, as to the true location of the boundary line separating Parcel One and Parcel Two. To resolve that uncertainty, Party One and Party Two agree that the boundary line between Parcel One and Parcel Two is fixed and established as follows: the existing fence line running north-south between the two parcels.

This document does not convey, transfer, or grant any interest in real property from either party to the other, and does not enlarge or diminish either party's parcel; it records Party One's and Party Two's own agreement as to the location of an existing, but previously uncertain, boundary line between Parcel One and Parcel Two.

THE AGREED-BOUNDARY DOCTRINE: A COMMON-LAW RULE FOR FIXING AN UNCERTAIN LINE
California recognizes a doctrine, developed by California courts rather than set out in a statute, under which adjoining landowners who are uncertain where the true boundary line between their parcels actually lies may fix that line by their own agreement. Secondary legal commentary describing this doctrine (identified in this clause's gap, since the underlying case law itself could not be independently verified in this research session) states it as requiring three things: (1) an uncertainty as to the true boundary line between the parcels, as distinct from a mere disagreement about a boundary both parties otherwise know the true location of; (2) an agreement, express or implied, between the adjoining owners fixing where the line is; and (3) acceptance and acquiescence in the line so fixed, described in that commentary either as lasting for a period equal to the applicable statute of limitations, or as arising under circumstances where changing the line's position would cause substantial loss. California's general statute of limitations for an action to recover real property, or its possession, is five years, running from when the plaintiff (or the plaintiff's predecessor or grantor) was last seized or possessed of the property. Where this doctrine applies, secondary commentary states that the agreed line becomes the boundary between the parcels, even if a survey conducted from the calls in the parties' deeds would show a different line. This document's boundary line agreement declaration does not itself transfer, convey, or grant any interest in real property from one party to the other; it records the parties' own statement of where an existing, but previously uncertain, boundary line lies.

DISTINCT FROM ADVERSE POSSESSION: A DIFFERENT LEGAL THEORY FOR A BOUNDARY DISPUTE
California's Code of Civil Procedure separately sets out a statutory basis on which a person may establish adverse possession of land, a legal theory analytically distinct from the agreed-boundary doctrine described elsewhere in this document. Under that statute, land is deemed to have been possessed and occupied, for adverse-possession purposes, only where it has been protected by a substantial enclosure or has been usually cultivated or improved; and in no case is adverse possession established unless the land has been occupied and claimed continuously for five years, with the claimant, or the claimant's predecessors and grantors, having timely paid all state, county, or municipal taxes levied and assessed on the land during that five-year period. This statutory test centers on a claimant's own possession, improvement, and tax payment with respect to land, regardless of whether the claimant and the neighboring owner ever agreed on, or were ever uncertain about, where the true boundary line lay. The agreed-boundary doctrine addresses a different starting condition: the adjoining owners' shared uncertainty about where the true boundary line is, resolved by their own agreement fixing it, rather than one owner's occupation of land the parties know, or could know, belongs to someone else. A landowner facing a boundary encroachment or dispute may have more than one potentially available legal theory on a given set of facts, of which adverse possession and the agreed-boundary doctrine are two; this clause states each as a distinct, separately sourced fact about California law, not as a determination of which theory, if any, applies to a specific dispute.

NO BOUNDARY-SPECIFIC RECORDING STATUTE; GENERAL RECORDING RULES APPLY
California does not have a statute that specifically addresses a "boundary line agreement," or a boundary line agreement's recordation, as its own distinct category of instrument; the agreed-boundary doctrine described elsewhere in this document is a common-law doctrine, not a creature of statute. A written agreement fixing a previously uncertain boundary line is, like other written instruments affecting an interest in real property, recorded under California's general recording statutes rather than any boundary-specific one. Once validly signed, such an agreement is effective as between the parties who signed it whether or not it is ever recorded; recording is not a condition of its validity between those parties. Recording matters for what it does against later claimants: California law states that every conveyance of real property, once acknowledged, certified, and recorded as prescribed by law, serves from the time it is filed with the recorder as constructive notice of its contents to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees, and California is a "race-notice" state, under which an earlier, unrecorded conveyance of the same property is void against a later purchaser or mortgagee who takes in good faith, for valuable consideration, and records first. Separately, California law provides a specific exemption, under the Subdivision Map Act, for a "lot line adjustment" between four or fewer existing adjoining parcels, subject to local agency or advisory agency approval limited to a determination of conformance with the local general plan and zoning and building ordinances. That lot line adjustment process is a different statutory mechanism, addressing a deliberate reconfiguration of recorded lot lines for land-use and mapping purposes; it is not the common-law agreed-boundary doctrine described elsewhere in this document, and this document's boundary line agreement declaration is not drafted to accomplish, and does not substitute for, a Subdivision Map Act lot line adjustment.

LEGAL DESCRIPTION SUFFICIENCY FOR RECORDING AND NOTICE TO LATER PURCHASERS
California law requires a county recorder to accept for recordation an instrument affecting real property, on payment of proper fees and taxes, if the instrument contains sufficient information to be indexed as provided by statute, meets state and local recording requirements, and is photographically reproducible; the recorder may not refuse to record it on the basis of the instrument's "lack of legal sufficiency." Because both indexing and constructive notice to later purchasers depend on a recorded document identifying the real property it affects, a boundary line agreement that is meant to describe a specific, locatable line, and to give notice of that line to anyone who later takes an interest in either parcel, typically references a legal description sufficient to locate the agreed line on the ground, rather than relying on a street address alone. As a practical matter, describing a boundary line's specific location is often accompanied by a survey or other technical description prepared for that purpose. This is a factual point about what makes a recorded instrument identify real property adequately for indexing and later notice under California's general recording statutes; it is not a determination that a survey is required by statute in every case, and it does not evaluate the adequacy of any specific legal description.

California's race-notice recording rule is stated here as evidence of how one state resolves competing claims to the same property, not as a claim about which state's recording rule governs a particular property or agreement — recording statutes vary by state, including "pure race" and "pure notice" states. This clause treats a boundary line agreement as a "conveyance of real property" within §§ 1213 and 1214's own words for purposes of the general recording rule; it does not independently verify, through case law, every circumstance in which an unrecorded boundary line agreement in fact binds or does not bind a later purchaser of either parcel. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's general recording framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property.

expectedJSON.body: California law requires a county recorder to accept for recordation an instrument affecting real property, on payment of proper fees and taxes, if the instrument contains sufficient information to be indexed as provided by statute, meets state and local recording requirements, and is photographically reproducible; the recorder may not refuse to record it on the basis of the instrument's "lack of legal sufficiency." Because both indexing and constructive notice to later purchasers depend on a recorded document identifying the real property it affects, a boundary line agreement that is meant to describe a specific, locatable line, and to give notice of that line to anyone who later takes an interest in either parcel, typically references a legal description sufficient to locate the agreed line on the ground, rather than relying on a street address alone. As a practical matter, describing a boundary line's specific location is often accompanied by a survey or other technical description prepared for that purpose. This is a factual point about what makes a recorded instrument identify real property adequately for indexing and later notice under California's general recording statutes; it is not a determination that a survey is required by statute in every case, and it does not evaluate the adequacy of any specific legal description.

citations.cite: California Government Code, recorder's duty to accept a conforming instrument that contains sufficient information to be indexed
citations.quote: The recorder shall, upon payment of proper fees and taxes, accept for recordation any instrument, paper, or notice that is authorized or required by statute, or court order to be recorded, or authorized or required to be recorded by a local ordinance that relates to the recordation of any instrument, paper, or notice that relates to real property, if the instrument, paper, or notice contains sufficient information to be indexed as provided by statute, meets recording requirements of state statutes and local ordinances, and is photographically reproducible. The county recorder shall not refuse to record any instrument, paper, or notice that is authorized or required by statute, court order, or local ordinance that relates to the recordation of any instrument, paper, or notice that relates to real property to be recorded on the basis of its lack of legal sufficiency.

Gov't Code § 27201(a)(1)(A); no additional independent statutory source was found requiring a "sufficient" legal description specifically for a boundary line agreement, so this clause's practical point about legal descriptions is drawn from § 27201(a)(1)(A)'s general indexing requirement, read together with the constructive-notice rule of Cal. Civ. Code § 1213 (independently cited and verified in a separate clause of this document, and not re-cited here as a second source for this clause). This is California's own recording-formalities framework; acknowledgment, indexing, and recording mechanics are not uniform across states, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs a particular boundary line agreement or parcel. This clause does not address any particular county recorder's additional local formatting requirements (margins, page size, first-page content, and similar mechanics), which § 27201(a)(1)(A) itself contemplates may exist on top of this statewide framework.
